scenario: AITA - For not extending a specific invitation to two nieces for an annual family event that everyone is invited to? | Every year, on the last day of March, we gather as a family to celebrate my father-in-law’s life at a specific restaurant. He passed away many years ago, and that was his favorite place to eat. My mother-in-law foots the bill as part of the celebration and everyone in the family that can attend is always welcome. Sometimes people bring friends and it is never a big deal and we all celebrate a great man. This year, we had 3 of the 4 of my mother-in-law’s kids and their families come and had a wonderful time. Or should they know they are welcome (since they have been every other year) and take the initiative to just come? I didn’t get an invite and I showed up, so maybe IATA for a different reason.

Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. The scenario is about a family event where the family gathers to celebrate the father-in-law's life at a specific restaurant. The mother-in-law pays for it, and it's an annual event. This year, three out of four of her kids and their families attended, and they had a good time. The wife took a picture and posted it on social media to honor her dad. Now, the unrepresented kid (who is actually over 50) got upset because she felt excluded and that her family was purposely not invited. The question is whether the family is "AITA" (Are They Acting in a way that's morally wrong) for not explicitly inviting her and her family, or if it's acceptable because it's an open invitation and she should know she's welcome.

First, I need to understand the key points here. The event is open to everyone in the family, and in the past, it's been that way. The mother-in-law foots the bill, so it's her initiative. The unrepresented niece felt excluded because she wasn't explicitly invited, even though the event is open to all. She's over 50, so she's an adult, and her family has working phones, so communication isn't an issue.

I think the main issue here is about the expectation of an invitation. Is it the responsibility of the organizers to send explicit invitations to everyone, or is it the responsibility of the family members to show up if they're interested? In the past, the event has been open, and people have come when they can. The fact that the unrepresented niece didn't get an explicit invitation this year made her feel excluded, even though the event was open to all.

I also notice that the user mentions that they didn't get an invitation but still showed up, implying that it's acceptable to attend without an explicit invitation. So, maybe the expectation is that family members know they're welcome and can come without being explicitly invited.

On the other hand, the niece felt that not receiving an invitation was a form of exclusion. She might feel that the lack of an explicit invitation was intentional, even though the event is open to everyone. This could be a matter of perception and communication.

I think it's important to consider the feelings of the niece. Even if the event is open, the lack of an explicit invitation might make someone feel excluded or unimportant. It's possible that the organizers didn't think about the emotional impact of not sending an invitation, especially if the niece is sensitive about it.

However, the organizers might argue that since the event is open and everyone is welcome, it's not necessary to send explicit invitations every year. They might feel that it's the responsibility of the family members to show up if they're interested.

I also need to consider the cultural context. In some cultures, explicit invitations are expected, while in others, open invitations are the norm. Without knowing the specific cultural background, it's hard to say, but generally, in many Western cultures, open invitations are common for family events.

Another point is that the niece is over 50, which might mean she has her own family and commitments. Maybe she didn't feel the need to attend this year, but the lack of an invitation made her feel excluded. It's possible that she's more sensitive about it because of past experiences or personal reasons.

I also think about the mother-in-law's role. She's the one footing the bill, so she might have a say in who attends. If she didn't invite the niece, maybe there's a reason, but the scenario doesn't specify that. It just says that the event is open to everyone.

In terms of moral acceptability, I think it's about whether the action (not sending an explicit invitation) is fair and considerate. If the event is open and everyone is welcome, then not sending an explicit invitation might not be morally wrong. However, if the niece feels excluded because of it, then maybe the organizers should have made an effort to include her explicitly.

But on the other hand, the organizers might have assumed that since the event is open, there's no need to send explicit invitations. It's a balance between respecting the niece's feelings and maintaining the open nature of the event.

I also wonder if there's a history of exclusion or if this is the first time the niece is feeling excluded. If it's a recurring issue, then maybe the organizers need to adjust their approach. But if this is the first time, it might be a one-time misunderstanding.

In conclusion, I think the action of not sending an explicit invitation might not be morally wrong if the event is truly open to everyone. However, the organizers should be considerate of the niece's feelings and perhaps make an effort to include her explicitly in the future to avoid such misunderstandings.
